title: Nathan Straus opened pasteurized milk stations for the children of New York, and infant mortality fell

trailer.text: Nathan Straus (1848–1931) was a Jewish philanthropist and social activist, and co-owner of two large department stores in New York.
He and his wife Lina lost their toddler daughter Sara to milk that was likely contaminated.
In 1892, after consulting with physicians, Straus launched a campaign for the pasteurization of milk, and later set up low-cost milk stations for the city's poor.
The stations sold sterilized and refrigerated milk below wholesale prices, or gave it free to those who could not pay.

According to the estimate of the city's Department of Health, thanks to the work done in the campaign for clean milk in the years 1892–1925, the lives of more than 400,000 New York children under the age of five were saved.

stations.title: Before: a city where babies die

paragraphs.text: Nathan Straus was born in Otterberg on January 31, 1848, to a German Jewish family.
He grew up in Georgia and strongly identified as a Jew.
He later became co-owner of two large department stores in New York.
In the New York of that time, about a quarter of babies died before their first birthday.
There was mourning in the Straus home as well. He and his wife Lina lost their toddler daughter Sara to milk that was likely contaminated.
According to one source, he was particularly sensitive to child mortality because of the deaths of his children.

In the early 1890s a cow he kept at his camp in the Adirondacks suddenly died, and an autopsy found that it had tuberculosis. After this, Straus immediately saw to it that his own children drank pasteurized milk.

stations.title: The laboratory and the milk stations

paragraphs.text: In 1892, after consulting with physicians, Straus launched a campaign for the pasteurization of milk.
That same year he opened the pasteurized milk laboratory named after him.
Later he set up the first low-cost milk stations for the city's poor.
According to one source, this was the first infant milk station in America.
Pasteurized milk was then an expensive product.
Straus and Lina supplied it at affordable prices: a penny a glass, two cents a pint and four cents a quart.
The stations sold sterilized and refrigerated milk below wholesale prices, or gave it to those who could not pay.
According to Fisher, Straus himself designed and funded the milk stations in Manhattan.
The stations opened in every district of Manhattan.
Straus established, at his own expense, 297 milk stations in 36 cities.
Over 25 years, more than 24 million glasses and bottles of safe milk were distributed.
Of 20,111 children fed on pasteurized milk supplied by Straus over four years, only six died.
In 1898 the death rate at the city orphanage fell to 20 percent, with pasteurized milk the only change.
According to a report by the U.S. Treasury Department, the pasteurization of milk quickly cut the death rate of children under five in half.
According to an estimate by New York's health commissioner, infant deaths fell by two-thirds in the first two decades of the 20th century.
According to John Steele Gordon in the journal Philanthropy, the national infant death rate fell from 125.1 per thousand in 1891 to 15.8 in 1925.

stations.title: Cities require pasteurization, and the world listens

paragraphs.text: According to one source, by 1908 the infant death rate had already been cut in half thanks to voluntary pasteurization.
Afterwards Chicago became the first American city to require pasteurization, and later New York required it as well.
According to one source, the infant death rate in New York fell to 90 per thousand in 1914, after the city required the pasteurization of all milk.
In Europe, Straus began his work by establishing a pasteurization plant in Heidelberg in 1907.
In 1909 he opened a tuberculosis preventorium for children in Lakewood, New Jersey; the facility was later moved to Farmingdale.
In 1911 President Taft appointed him the sole United States delegate to the International Congress for the Protection of Infants in Berlin.
According to Fisher, after a visit in 1904 Straus became an ardent supporter of establishing a Jewish homeland in the Middle East.
He brought two Hadassah nurses to the Land of Israel and settled them in Jerusalem.
According to JTA, malaria there was a constant threat to Jews and Arabs alike.
Straus spent $325,000 on the two health centers in Jerusalem and Tel Aviv.
He also made possible the establishment of the Pasteur Institute.
According to later accounts, Straus and Hadassah laid foundations for the health system of the modern State of Israel.
The Israeli city of Netanya is named after him.
The city's founders hoped he would contribute to its development, but Straus no longer had anything left to give.
Straus distributed more than one and a half million buckets of coal, and even obtained permission to use the city's piers for his coal depots.
Out of regard for human dignity, he charged 5 cents for the relief tickets to those who could pay, and gave them free to those who could not.
When members of the Straus family were refused admission to a hotel in Lakewood because they were Jews, Straus bought adjacent land and built a hotel on it open to all.
He publicly called on Henry Ford to submit the "Protocols of the Elders of Zion" to an impartial jury.
In 1894 Straus was offered the nomination for mayor, but he did not run.
According to the Berman Jewish Policy Archive, he was offered the Democratic nomination and declined
The editor Arthur Brisbane said that when asked who had done the most for the protection of the child, one must point to a Jew.
People praised Straus for doing more for the children of New York than any other person.
According to Fisher, his work won praise from four U.S. presidents and from figures such as Albert Einstein.
In 1923, marking 25 years since the founding of Greater New York, Straus was chosen by popular vote as the resident who had made the greatest contribution to public welfare in the city.
Unlike many others, Straus gave the bulk of his fortune to charity during his lifetime.
He died in Manhattan on January 11, 1931, a few weeks before his 83rd birthday.
His estate amounted to about a million dollars, because he had already given away most of his wealth, and he left nothing to charity.
Thousands of people came to his funeral.
According to Fisher, Straus overcame fierce opposition from the dairy industry.
From pediatricians and elected officials he met both opposition and support.
Dairy farmers, milk dealers and distributors did not want to pay the cost of pasteurization.
Supporters of "certified milk" opposed pasteurization because it kills only 99 percent of the organisms in milk, not all of them.
Critics argued that the city had neither the money nor the infrastructure for mandatory pasteurization, which Straus and Jacobi supported.
Some critics doubted Straus's claim that pasteurization helped against infant mortality.
In 1897 he was arrested and brought before the Court of Special Sessions.
In 1910, hurt by the criticism, Straus decided to close his milk stations in New York.
After a wave of public support he reversed his decision, and the stations remained open for a few more years.

claims.text: חקלאי חלב, סוחרי חלב ומפיצים לא רצו לשאת בעלות הפיסטור.
claims.quote: many dairymen, farmers and commercial milk distributors were disinclined to assume the expense of pasteurization

claims.text: תומכי החלב המוסמך התנגדו לפיסטור כי הוא אינו הורג כל אורגניזם בחלב אלא רק 99 אחוז מהם.
claims.quote: The movement for certified milk objected to pasteurization because it did not kill every organism in milk, only 99 percent of them

claims.text: מבקרים טענו שלעיר אין הכסף והתשתית להנהיג פיסטור חובה, כפי ששטראוס וג'ייקובי תמכו.
claims.quote: critics, who argued that the city had neither the money nor the infrastructure to institute mandatory pasteurization

claims.text: חלק ממבקריו פקפקו בכך שפיסטור יעיל נגד תמותת תינוקות כפי שהוא טען.
claims.quote: Some of his critics were rather dubious that pasteurization was as effective at combating infant mortality as he made it out to be.

claims.text: לפי המקור, שטראוס נעצר ב-1897, הובא בפני בית הדין לדיונים מיוחדים והורשע בהגשת חלב.
claims.quote: he was arrested in 1897 and brought before the Manhattan Court of Special Sessions and convicted of serving

claims.text: לפי המקור, יריביו גרמו למעצרו ולהבאתו לבית הדין בטענה שמיהל חלב, טענה שנבעה מכך שבחלק מהתחנות החלב עובד לתזונת תינוקות.
claims.quote: Once his opponents caused him to be arrested and haled before the Court of Special Sessions, on the charge of having watered milk

claims.text: ב-1910, פגוע מהביקורת, החליט שטראוס לסגור את תחנות החלב שלו בניו יורק.
claims.quote: Straus decided in 1910 to shut down his milk depots in New York once and for all

claims.text: אחרי גל תמיכה ציבורי חזר בו שטראוס והשאיר את תחנות החלב פתוחות עוד כמה שנים.
claims.quote: Straus rescinded his earlier decision and kept open his milk stations for a few more years.

claims.text: לפי מאמר ב-Distillations, בשנת 1891 עמד שיעור תמותת התינוקות בניו יורק על 240 מקרי מוות לכל 1,000 לידות.
claims.quote: In 1891 the infant mortality rate for New York City averaged 240 deaths per every 1,000 births.

claims.text: לפי פישר, בראשית שנות ה-90 של המאה ה-19 עמד שיעור התמותה השנתי של ילדים מתחת לגיל חמש בניו יורק על כ-15 אחוז.
claims.quote: the annual mortality rate among children under five was about 15 percent

claims.text: בין 1878 ל-1893 איבדו נתן ולינה שלושה ילדים למחלות.
claims.quote: Between 1878 and 1893, Nathan and his beloved wife Lina lost three children to disease

claims.text: ב-1893, על חשבונו, פתח שטראוס את הראשונה מבין 18 תחנות חלב בניו יורק.
claims.quote: In 1893, and at his own expense, Straus opened the first of 18 milk distribution depots throughout New York City

claims.text: לפי ההערכה, מאמציו של שטראוס הצילו ישירות את חייהם של 445,800 ילדים.
claims.quote: Altogether it is estimated that the efforts of Nathan Straus directly saved the lives of 445,800 children.

claims.text: לפי Jewish Press, כבר ב-1912 הניח שטראוס את יסודות פעילות הבריאות בארץ ישראל והקים מחלקת בריאות.
claims.quote: He also laid the foundation of the work for public health in Eretz Yisrael with which his name would later become prominently associated by founding a Health Department

claims.text: לפי המקור, מ-1913 נתן שטראוס יותר משני שלישים מהונו למוסדות ולאנשים יהודים בארץ ישראל.
claims.quote: Beginning with his return to the land in 1913, Nathan gave more than two-thirds of his vast fortune to Jewish institutions and individuals there

claims.text: לפי הערכת היסטוריונים, שטראוס נתן יותר ממחצית הונו לפיתוח ישראל.
claims.quote: Some historians have estimated that he gave more than half his fortune toward the development of Israel.

claims.text: לפי Jewish Press, שטראוס עיכב את חזרתו כי הרגיש שיש לו עוד הרבה עבודה למען יהודי ארץ ישראל.
claims.quote: Nathan again delayed because he felt he had so much more work to do on behalf of Jews in Eretz Yisrael

claims.text: ב-1909 פתח פרוונטוריום לילדים נגד שחפת בלייקווד, ניו ג'רזי, ואחר כך הועבר המקום לפארמינגדייל.
claims.quote: a refuge was provided for the children near Farmingdale, N. J., and they were cared for in the farm house until permanent

claims.text: הוא גם אפשר את הקמת מכון פסטר.
claims.quote: He also established a Pasteur Institute in Eretz Yisrael.

claims.text: מייסדי העיר קיוו שיתרום לפיתוחה, אבל לשטראוס כבר לא נשאר מה לתת.
claims.quote: Alas, they came too late, as Straus had no more money to contribute.

claims.text: מייסדי העיר קיוו שיתרום לפיתוחה, אבל לשטראוס כבר לא נשאר מה לתת.
claims.quote: the hope was that by naming the city after him, Straus would bequeath additional funds to this new settlement.

claims.text: הוא מת במנהטן ב-11 בינואר 1931, כמה שבועות לפני יום הולדתו ה-83.
claims.quote: Straus died on January 11, 1931, in Manhattan.

claims.text: 250,000 דולר למרכז בירושלים
claims.quote: Nathan Straus has given $250,000 for the creation of a Health Center in Jerusalem

claims.text: הוא שבר רגל בביקור בפלשתינה ב-1912
claims.quote: He broke his leg during a 1912 visit to Palestine and was therefore unable to join his brother Isidor
